summary: Describes the Internet Key Exchange, a hybrid protocol that negotiates security associations and produces authenticated keying material for IPsec. It combines pieces of ISAKMP and OAKLEY. This first version is now historic, replaced by RFC 4306.

eli5.summary: Before two computers can talk privately, they must agree on a shared secret without anyone overhearing. IKE is the careful conversation they have to do that.

subtitle: The original IPsec key exchange: two phases that set up a protected channel and then negotiate fresh keys for IPsec.

tldr.problem: ISAKMP provides a framework for authentication and key exchange but does not define the exchanges themselves, so IPsec needed a concrete way to negotiate security associations and authenticated keys.
tldr.mechanism: IKE combines part of Oakley and part of SKEME with ISAKMP. In phase 1, Main Mode or Aggressive Mode builds an authenticated ISAKMP SA using Diffie-Hellman; in phase 2, Quick Mode negotiates the SAs for services such as AH and ESP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2409 is now Historic. It was replaced by RFC 4306 and updated by RFC 4109.

today: RFC 2409 is Historic. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4306 and updated by RFC 4109, so the newer RFC is the one to read for current IKE.

sections.title: What IKE Is
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange (IKE) is a hybrid protocol. It takes part of Oakley and part of SKEME and runs them inside the ISAKMP framework to negotiate, and produce authenticated keying material for, security associations. Those can be ISAKMP's own, or ones for AH and ESP under the IETF IPsec DOI.

The RFC says it can be used to set up virtual private networks and to give a remote user, whose IP address need not be known beforehand, access to a secure host or network. It also supports client negotiation, where the negotiating parties are not the endpoints, and in that mode the identities of the end parties stay hidden.

IKE does not implement all of Oakley or all of SKEME and does not depend on either.
sections.eli5: IKE is a secret handshake that two computers do before they start whispering. At the end they both know the same secret key, and nobody else does.

sections.title: Phases, Modes and Negotiated Attributes
sections.content:
IKE works in two phases. Phase 1 sets up a secure, authenticated channel called the ISAKMP SA, using Main Mode or Aggressive Mode. Phase 2 negotiates SAs on behalf of services such as IPsec, using Quick Mode. New Group Mode is neither phase and may only follow phase 1. A single phase 1 can serve several phase 2 negotiations, and a single phase 2 can request multiple SAs.

Phase 1 negotiates four mandatory attributes: an encryption algorithm, a hash algorithm, an authentication method and a Diffie-Hellman group. A pseudo-random function can optionally be negotiated, otherwise the HMAC version of the hash is used.

Implementations MUST support DES in CBC mode, MD5 and SHA, pre-shared key authentication and MODP group number one. They SHOULD support 3DES, Tiger, the Digital Signature Standard, RSA signatures and RSA public key encryption, and MODP group number 2. Main Mode MUST be implemented and Aggressive Mode SHOULD be.
sections.eli5: First the two computers build a small private room together. Then, whenever they need a new lock, they go into that room and make it there, which is quick.

sections.title: Phase 1: Main Mode and Aggressive Mode
sections.content:
Main Mode takes six messages: the first two negotiate policy, the next two exchange Diffie-Hellman public values and nonces, and the last two authenticate the exchange and carry the identities, which are encrypted and so protected. Aggressive Mode takes three messages. It saves round trips but gives up identity protection (except with public key encryption) and cannot negotiate the Diffie-Hellman group.

Four authentication methods work with either mode: digital signatures, two forms of public key encryption, and a pre-shared key. Each computes a base value called SKEYID differently, then derives three keys from it: SKEYID_d for deriving keys for other SAs, SKEYID_a for authenticating the ISAKMP SA and SKEYID_e for encrypting it. The initiator and responder prove themselves with HASH_I and HASH_R.

With a pre-shared key in Main Mode, the key can only be identified by the peers' IP addresses, because the initiator must compute HASH_I before it has processed the responder's identity.
sections.eli5: Main Mode is a careful, slow introduction where you hide your name until you are sure who you are talking to. Aggressive Mode is a quick one where you shout your name right away.

sections.title: Phase 2: Quick Mode and Forward Secrecy
sections.content:
Quick Mode is protected by the ISAKMP SA, so everything after the ISAKMP header is encrypted. It is a three-message exchange of SA proposals and nonces, authenticated by HASH(1), HASH(2) and HASH(3). The nonces give replay protection and freshness. One exchange can negotiate several SAs at once, and each negotiated SA yields one inbound and one outbound association.

New keying material is derived as KEYMAT = prf(SKEYID_d, protocol | SPI | Ni_b | Nr_b). If the optional KE payload is sent, an extra Diffie-Hellman exchange is done and its secret is mixed in, which gives perfect forward secrecy (PFS) for the keys. Base Quick Mode without KE refreshes keys but does not provide PFS.

For PFS of both keys and identities, a peer MUST establish only one non-ISAKMP SA per ISAKMP SA, then delete the ISAKMP SA.
sections.eli5: Once you are in the private room, making a new key is fast. If you want an extra-safe key, you do one more secret-number swap so an old key can never unlock new things.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Groups and Other Exchanges
sections.content:
Four Oakley groups are defined. Group 1 is a MODP group with a 768-bit prime that implementations MUST support. Group 2 is a MODP group with a 1024-bit prime that implementations SHOULD support. Groups 3 and 4 are elliptic curve groups over GF[2^155] and GF[2^185], which implementations SHOULD support. Values of 2^15 and higher identify private groups.

New Group Mode lets two peers define a private group after phase 1 so that only its identifier, not its parameters, crosses the wire in the clear during phase 1. ISAKMP Informational Exchanges (Notify or Delete) are protected by a HASH once the ISAKMP SA exists, and are sent in the clear if it does not yet exist.
sections.eli5: The groups are like a menu of different secret-number games. The numbers inside a game are huge, and bigger games are harder to crack.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Hints
sections.content:
The RFC says confidentiality and authentication are only as good as the attributes negotiated for the ISAKMP SA. Repeated Quick Mode re-keying can consume the entropy of the Diffie-Hellman secret, so implementers should limit the number of Quick Mode exchanges between exponentiations, though no limit is set. Group one with a strong random number generator and an exponent of no less than 160 bits is called sufficient for DES, and groups two to four provide greater security. Diffie-Hellman exponents are assumed to be erased after use.

The last round trip of Main Mode is encrypted but not strictly authenticated, so an active substitution attack could corrupt optional payloads undetected. Implementation hints include caching phase 1 state to avoid exponentiations, pre-establishing SAs, and not responding to Informational exchanges, to avoid a "notify war".
sections.eli5: A secret is only as strong as the weakest piece you chose. So pick strong pieces, throw away the temporary numbers, and do not keep replying to each other's error messages forever.
